summary:
The Pitcairn Islands are a British Overseas Territory. Defence and external affairs are reserved to the United Kingdom, and United Kingdom domestic measures, including the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code on single-sex services, do not apply in Pitcairn of their own force; they could reach the territory only by Order in Council. Local law governs.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001, so a visitor faces no criminalisation exposure on that ground.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, in force since 2010. The guarantee is constitutional rather than an offence provision, and it names sexual orientation, not gender identity.

Marriage has been legal for two people of the same sex since 14 May 2015. Local law defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, so the definition does not turn on a spouse's sex or gender identity. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 also recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn.

The ordinance was approved unanimously by the Island Council on 1 April 2015, signed by Governor Jonathan Sinclair on 5 May 2015 and published on 13 May 2015.
tangentialFactors:
The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 and the 2015 marriage ordinance diverge in scope. The marriage definition names gender identity; the anti-discrimination guarantee names only sexual orientation. The sources identify no local provision extending the discrimination guarantee to gender identity or gender expression.

Legislative competence sits with the Island Council, with the Governor assenting, and United Kingdom legislation reaches the territory only by Order in Council. The territory is indexed within United Kingdom LGBT-rights timelines, and its marriage and adoption provisions sit alongside that parent framework rather than deriving from it.
localsOnly:
Adoption is open to married, unmarried and single people.

Military service is a United Kingdom responsibility rather than a local one.

None of the roughly 50 residents is publicly known to be in a same-sex relationship.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory rests on encyclopaedic republications of a single article. No primary legal text, court record or enforcement data was consulted.

No entry, visa or documentation rules specific to trans travellers are sourced, and no account of how a trans visitor's documents would be handled at entry was identified.

No trans-specific violence, hate-crime provision, facilities rule or healthcare access rule for the Pitcairn Islands appears in the sources.
